name: Anti-establishment
summary: Anti-establishment politics opposes a society's conventional ruling institutions and principles, casting the political, economic and cultural elite as corrupt and out of touch with ordinary people. It is a stance rather than a program, used by 1960s counterculture and the New Left, by Occupy and the Seattle protesters, and in the 2010s mostly by right-wing populists. Its positions on the economy, culture and immigration come from whatever ideology it is attached to.
scope: The shared core across strands: elite corruption, hostility to established institutions and experts, and preference for direct popular decision-making, drawn from the 1892 Omaha Platform, Wikipedia's account of anti-establishment views, and Cas Mudde's definition of populism. It does not take a single left or right strand, so most economic and social answers are neutral and low-confidence.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Left-wing anti-establishment movements such as Occupy would say yes, right-wing ones are mixed, so the stance does not settle it.

public-ownership.rationale: The Omaha Platform wanted public railroads and telegraphs, but modern right-wing anti-establishment parties do not, so adherents split.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Occupy-style left strands say yes and right strands are mixed; the Omaha Platform's graduated income tax is one precedent.

unions-good.rationale: Left strands side with unions; right-wing populists often court workers but distrust union leadership as an establishment.

property-fundamental.rationale: No defining position; the strands differ on property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporations count as part of the establishment for the left, while right strands target government and media more, so the answer splits.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare policy comes from the host ideology, not the anti-establishment stance.

worker-ownership.rationale: A left-strand idea absent from the right-wing strand.

legalize-drugs.rationale: 1960s counterculture opposed harsh drug laws, while 2010s right-wing strands do not share that view.

state-harmful.rationale: Anti-establishment views oppose those who hold power, not the state as such; only anarchist strands say it is harmful.

limit-guns.rationale: Strands split: American right-wing strands oppose limits, left strands may favor them.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

reviewHistory.rationale: Police and military are establishment institutions, but right-wing strands support them; adherents split.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

legalize-sex-work.rationale: A social question without a stance-based answer.

rehabilitation.rationale: Host-dependent: left strands favor it, right strands punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: Social conservatism is a host-ideology matter; 1960s counterculture rejected conventional norms while 2010s right-wing strands defend them.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: 1960s liberation strands supported gay rights, while many right-wing strands oppose; adherents split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Not defined by the stance; religion is part of the establishment for some and of the people for others.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: 1960s strands opposed racial inequality, but right-wing strands now reject such policies as establishment orthodoxy.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Right-wing strands see this as a progressive establishment norm, left strands may accept it.

gradual-change.rationale: Anti-establishment views are defined by opposition to established principles and institutions, so respect for them is rejected.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Right-wing populists want it, left strands do not; the Omaha Platform opposed 'undesirable' immigration but this is not the core.

free-trade.rationale: The 1999 Seattle WTO protests were anti-establishment from the left and tariffs appeal to right strands too, so no consistent answer.

nation-first.rationale: Right strands say yes and left strands reject it.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Anti-war 1960s strands said no, but the stance does not decide it.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Right strands treat climate policy as elite agenda, left strands demand action; split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Some strands (1968 radicals) accept it, but most contemporary populist movements work through elections.

experts-over-public.rationale: Populism treats the people's common sense as superior to elite expertise, and the stance opposes the institutions that experts staff.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Host-dependent; left strands favor it, right strands do not.

basic-income.rationale: Left strands such as Occupy might back it, while right-wing strands tend to resist; the stance gives no answer.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Distrust of finance runs through the stance (Occupy, Omaha money plank), but other strands want central bank control of money.

democracy-best.rationale: Populists accept popular sovereignty and majority rule, unlike extremists who reject democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Populism favors direct decisions such as referendums, and the Omaha Platform endorsed initiative and referendum.

right-to-secede.rationale: Some outsider movements favor regional independence and others defend the nation; the stance does not decide.

political-violence-never.rationale: Strands differ from nonviolent protest movements to radical groups.

separate-church-state.rationale: Religion is a host-ideology matter, with secular left strands and religious right strands both anti-establishment.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Some right-wing strands want religious law while others do not, so the stance gives no answer.

military-superiority.rationale: Right strands favor it, 1960s strands opposed Cold War military spending.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Right-wing nativist hosts say yes and left strands no.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Left strands only; populism frames the divide as people versus elite rather than class.

restore-past-order.rationale: Right strands seek restoration while 1960s strands wanted change.

direct-action.rationale: Nulled: the statement now asks whether direct action should replace electoral politics (reworded 2026-11-10, Codex review). This answer rested on direct action used alongside elections or on a mixed record, which does not support agreeing that it should replace them; its sources need re-reading against the new text.

reviewHistory.rationale: Anti-establishment movements are associated with street protest such as 1968, Seattle and Occupy, though populists also use elections.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Left strands such as Occupy might agree and right strands would not.

media-academia-power.rationale: Right-wing anti-establishment strands see media and education as holding establishment power; left strands focus on finance, so contested.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Both strands distrust institutional knowledge, but only parts of the left put it as theory.

workplace-democracy.rationale: A left-strand idea that right-wing anti-establishment strands do not share.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education funding follows the host ideology, not the anti-elite stance.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy follows the host ideology; both austerity critics and deficit hawks use anti-elite language.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Populism often prefers common sense over expertise but takes no side on faith.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Right-wing strands favor it, left strands do not.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Social-conservative strands accept it and counterculture and liberation strands rejected it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Left strands agree; populism sees elites rather than class dominating.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Right strands favor it; left strands do not.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Right strands favor it, left strands do not.

elite-replacement.rationale: Some right-wing strands hold it but it is outside the stance's core and fringe for most adherents.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Left strands agree and right strands do not.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Corruption of and distance between the political class and ordinary people is the defining claim; the Omaha Platform says corruption dominates the ballot box and legislatures.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not part of the stance; coercive state control over families is inconsistent with the stance.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Left strands favor it, right strands defend security forces.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Strands differ by host ideology; the stance gives no answer.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Populism makes the general will of the people the goal of politics, so authority rests on popular consent.

population-transfer.rationale: Not part of the stance and inconsistent with mainstream populism, which accepts democratic limits, but some right strands differ.

separated-powers.rationale: Populists often accuse courts and media of being detached from the people, but the Omaha Platform sought checks through direct election of senators.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Left strands yes, right strands no.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Right strands favor it, left strands do not.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Counterculture and many outsider movements resist official cultural control; right strands may differ.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not part of the stance; populist leaders often seek long tenure but the stance opposes entrenched incumbents.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: 1960s strands opposed Cold War spending and right strands are split on alliances.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Omaha Platform came from farmers but the modern stance has no rural doctrine.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Right-wing anti-establishment strands portray education and expert classes as detached from ordinary people.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: 1960s counterculture rejected conformity, but right strands do not.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Nationalist strands favor reunification, but the stance itself does not address borders.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Left strands such as Occupy favour debt forgiveness while right-wing anti-establishment parties are mixed; the stance itself does not settle it.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Left anti-establishment movements link political and economic change while right populists stress sovereignty; the shared core is silent.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Populism distrusts unelected, expert-run institutions insulated from the people, and the Omaha Platform attacked the money power; adherents want elected government control.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: A territorial question the anti-elite stance does not settle; nationalist hosts say no and anti-war hosts say yes.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Left strands (Omaha Platform's public ownership of railroads) agree while right-wing strands defend property; the core is neutral.

precautionary-principle.rationale: The stance defines no environmental position; left strands favour precaution and right strands often oppose it.

collective-defense.rationale: Left and right anti-establishment movements disagree on alliances such as NATO, so the stance does not settle it.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Left strands favour curbing church power while right populists often ally with religious institutions; not settled by the stance.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Populists often favour a leader who takes sides, while others value a unifying figure; adherents split.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Position comes from the host ideology: separatists and unionists both appear among anti-establishment movements.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Flat taxes appear in right-populist programs while left anti-establishment movements favour progressive rates; split.

space-expansion.rationale: The stance is silent on space policy; adherents are split between space enthusiasm and a priority on Earth problems.

leader-cult.rationale: Right-populist movements often build leader cults while others reject them as establishment trappings; adherents split.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Anti-establishment politics is a stance; the answer depends on the host ideology.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Omaha Platform demands that land held by railroads and speculators be reclaimed for actual settlers.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Left and right strands differ, so no common answer follows from hostility to the establishment.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Left and right strands differ, so no common answer follows.

ban-cartels.rationale: The Omaha Platform attacks monopolies and corporate power over markets.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Wikipedia's account of populism notes hostility to courts and independent bodies that block the popular will.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Left strands favour quotas and right strands oppose them, so it is split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Host ideologies differ: protectionist right and internationalist left strands both occur.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Strands differ; most use electoral or protest means, with no common view.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The stance has no curricular position; left strands oppose national narratives and right strands favour them.

patriotic-education.rationale: Right-wing anti-establishment movements favour it and left counterculture opposes it.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Strands conflict, with right populists opposing preferences and left movements supporting them.

public-money-creation.rationale: The Omaha Platform demanded a national currency issued by the general government only, though other strands do not share this.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Left strands expect collapse and right strands do not; the stance does not settle it.

delink-world-market.rationale: Anti-globalisation left and nationalist right both attack integration, but the stance itself is not a trade doctrine.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Populists distrust courts and entrenched limits on majorities, yet the Omaha Platform sought constitutional reforms; split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Depends on the attached ideology; no core position.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Depends on the attached ideology; no core position.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Varies by attached ideology (left yes, right populists often no).

filial-duty.rationale: A stance rather than a program; traditional strands support it and counterculture strands reject it.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Left and right strands split, with populists often protectionist and others unconcerned; the stance does not settle it.

single-official-language.rationale: Right-wing strands favour it and left strands oppose it; the stance does not settle it.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Populist nationalists favour restriction while other strands do not.

corporate-influence.rationale: The Omaha Platform charges that corporations and wealth have corrupted government, and the stance casts the economic as well as political elite as corrupt.

job-guarantee.rationale: Economic programs come from the attached ideology, so this is neutral.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Populism casts a corrupt elite as the enemy, and conspiracy thinking is common, but targeting an ethnic minority comes from particular right-wing strands, not the shared core.

informal-organisation.rationale: Counterculture and Occupy used informal groups while populist movements use parties, so it is split.

religious-nation.rationale: Religion's role depends on the attached ideology.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The stance has no fiscal position; strands differ, with some regionalists wanting to keep revenue and others not.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Left strands like Occupy and the Omaha Platform lean to common ownership of key sectors while right strands defend property; the stance does not settle it.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Strands split on public versus private delivery; the Omaha Platform wanted public ownership but modern populists vary.

religion-illusion.rationale: Religion is not a defining issue; left strands are secular and right populists often defend religion.

treaties-binding.rationale: No documented position; strands differ on minority and indigenous claims.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Counterculture strands favoured communes but most modern populism seeks to capture existing states; split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Anti-establishment politics opposes elites and defends popular opposition; the Omaha Platform attacks the suppression of the people's voice.

reification.rationale: Left strands accept the idea and right strands do not; the stance itself settles nothing.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The stance is not tied to any religious position; attached ideologies vary from traditionalist to counterculture.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Omaha Platform condemns wealth concentrated in few hands, but right-populist anti-establishment movements of the 2010s do not share that economics, so strands differ.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Anti-establishment movements range from secular counterculture to religious populists, so adherents are split on state-led unbelief.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Some strands (New Left, anarchist) want policing abolished while right-wing populists want more of it; the stance itself takes no side.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Existential risk is not an anti-establishment theme, and populists often distrust expert-driven priorities; adherents are split.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Religious views vary with the host ideology, so the stance gives no answer on women in religious office.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Marriage authority comes from the host ideology, not from opposition to elites; traditionalist and counterculture strands differ.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Left strands support it and right populists oppose it; the stance itself settles nothing.

rent-control.rationale: Economic policy comes from the attached ideology, not from hostility to elites.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Left and right anti-establishment strands both criticise foreign bases for different reasons, but the stance does not require it.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Omaha tradition says wealth belongs to those who create it, but that is one left-populist strand and right-populist anti-establishment movements do not share it, so strands differ.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Right-wing strands endorse it, left strands do not; the stance is neutral.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Populism's moral framing of people against elite is sometimes cast in good-versus-evil terms, but religious framing is not general.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Right populists endorse ethnic economic preference and left anti-establishment movements reject it, so the stance is split.

independent-unions.rationale: Anti-establishment politics is a stance, not a program; attached ideologies differ on unions.

second-chamber.rationale: The Omaha Platform sought direct election of senators rather than abolition, and the stance gives no settled view on bicameralism.

municipal-property.rationale: Neither the Omaha Platform nor the stance as defined by Mudde sets out a view on communal ownership of production.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Preference for popular decision-making might favour local assemblies, but the sources give no view on confederations.

family-wage.rationale: An economic detail the stance does not address; adherents split by their attached ideology.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Distrust of regulators and distrust of drug companies both fit the stance, so it points both ways.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Nothing in the stance bears on this; it is a technocratic question on which adherents split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Counterculture and religious populists in the stance's range split on this, and it is not part of its core.

gm-crops.rationale: Anti-establishment strands split between distrust of agribusiness and distrust of expert-led environmental opposition.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Right-wing populist strands lean towards it and left strands against, so the stance itself is split.

racial-pride.rationale: Right-wing and left-wing strands differ and the core stance is indifferent.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Populist and anti-elite rhetoric often charges that elites and foreign powers act against the nation, and the sources say this is common though not defining.

free-public-college.rationale: Left strands favour it and right strands do not; the stance gives no economic position.

pollution-taxes.rationale: No position follows from hostility to elites; adherents split on environmental policy.

arms-reduction.rationale: The stance is not tied to a defence view; left and right strands differ.

capital-controls.rationale: Left strands favour controls on capital and right populists often too, but others oppose them; the stance alone settles nothing.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: 1960s counterculture and the New Left urged refusal of war while right-wing populists back the military; the stance itself is split.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Left strands such as Occupy back unions; right-wing populists are mixed; opposition to elites does not settle it.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: A welfare-design question the stance does not address; left and right variants differ.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Seattle-style protesters want the world economy remade for poorer countries while right-wing populists want national protection; the stance is split.

sacred-nation.rationale: Right-wing populists revere the nation while counterculture and left strands do not; adherents are split.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Occupy-style movements back relief while right-wing anti-establishment movements oppose it; the stance is split.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Elite-versus-periphery framing appeals to some adherents, but the stance takes no position on regional exploitation as such.

public-service-media.rationale: Left strands defend public media while populists of the right treat broadcasters as part of the establishment; split.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Left strands (counterculture, Occupy) and right populists split on nuclear arms; the stance itself takes no side.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance rights are not an anti-establishment issue; the stance takes its social positions from the host ideology.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Adherents split between libertarian-style tort liability and regulation of corporations; the stance sets neither.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Hereditary chiefs are an establishment of their own, but some populists favor customary authority against central elites; adherents split.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Left anti-establishment movements favor environment over business interests, right populists favor liberty; adherents split.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Right populists favor fixed sentences and distrust judges, while the left opposes mass incarceration; adherents split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Left and right anti-establishment strands differ on religion, so the stance gives no answer.

indirect-election.rationale: The Omaha Platform demanded direct popular election of senators and wider direct democracy against corrupt legislatures, and populism favours direct popular decision.

national-church-status.rationale: A state church is an establishment institution, but right-wing strands often defend it, so strands split.

simple-living.rationale: Position comes from the host ideology; counterculture strands favoured it and others did not.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Adherents are split: right-wing populists may support it while the New Left opposes it.

close-ties-china.rationale: Foreign alignment depends on the attached ideology, so adherents are split.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Economic positions come from the attached left or right strand.

self-ownership.rationale: The stance does not address it; strands differ.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Tax policy depends on the attached ideology; the 1892 Omaha Platform favoured a graduated income tax instead.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The attached strand determines this; adherents are split.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Populism as defined by Mudde sets the people against the elite and favours direct popular will over mediating institutions.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The Omaha Platform attacks corporate and railroad privilege and the stance casts elites as corrupt and favoured.

distribution-by-process.rationale: A stance against elites rather than a programme; whether outcomes are judged by process or equality depends on the host ideology.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Occupy-style left strands favour such a tax while right-wing populists do not, so adherents split.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Left and right anti-establishment strands disagree on how much racism still limits people.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Hostility to established institutions could support disobedience, but populists also stress the will of the people expressed through law; adherents split.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The economic content comes from the attached ideology; the Omaha Platform's producer focus is not shared by modern right-wing strands.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Left strands pair solidarity with workers against nationalism while right-wing populists embrace patriotism; adherents split.

material-over-identity.rationale: Whether to prioritise material or identity concerns depends on the host ideology, left or right.

missingStatements.text: Elected officials are bound by their party, donors and insiders rather than by the voters they represent.
missingStatements.rationale: The Omaha Platform charges that corruption dominates the ballot box and legislatures, and the stance holds that the political class serves insiders over the people.

notes: Anti-establishment is a stance whose meaning depends on who is the establishment, so strands answer differently. Wikipedia reports the term was mostly left-wing in 1968 and mostly right-wing populist in the 2010s. Expect the inclusion check to find few stated positions.
